finding.claim: Caller identity is taken raw from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header, so any HTTP client can act as any user with grants, including deleting or renaming files. Conditional on deployment: no proxy or signature check is in the repo.
finding.sink: views.py:17 ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") then del STORE[fid] (line 18); views.py:25 is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") then f["name"] = ... (line 27); acl.py:5 grants.get(user, [])

trace.note: g.user set from request header with no verification
grant lookup keyed by spoofable user string

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session cookie, or proxy-strip check in repo. Missing header yields None, which fails the grant check (not a bypass). Not exploitable if an upstream proxy always overwrites the header; that proxy is not present in repo.

verdict.guard_found: none blocking. The only controls are the grant checks: ensure_allowed at acl.py:8-10 aborts with 403 on failure (effective, but keyed on the same client-supplied identity), and is_allowed at acl.py:4-5 is tested at views.py:25. Missing header yields None, which gets [] from grants and is denied, but any client can send any user string. No signature, session, or proxy-strip check exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: views.py:11 copies the raw X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user, views.py:17 passes it to ensure_allowed, acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, and views.py:18 deletes STORE[fid]. An anonymous HTTP client can therefore act as any granted user, though exploitation assumes the app is deployed without a proxy that always overwrites that header, which the repo cannot show.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (500) before any authorization check, while existing-but-forbidden IDs return 403, letting unauthenticated callers enumerate which file IDs exist.
finding.source: views.py:14 and views.py:22 URL segment <fid> — attacker-controlled path parameter
finding.sink: views.py:16 and views.py:24 STORE[fid] lookup (existence oracle via status code difference)

trace.note: abort(403) for existing but unauthorized resource

finding.guards_checked: Authorization is enforced on the actual operation, so this is an existence leak rather than a bypass. No try/except or 404 handling around the lookup.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:9-11 (before_request) only copies the X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user and never rejects requests. views.py:16 and views.py:24 index STORE[fid] with no try/except or .get, so a missing key raises KeyError before any check runs. acl.py:4-5 is_allowed returns False for unknown users, but it is never reached for missing IDs. acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed does abort(403), but only for existing resources.
verdict.reason: Unknown IDs hit STORE[fid] at views.py:16 (and :24) with no guard and produce a 500, while existing IDs fail the ACL check at acl.py:10 or views.py:26 with a 403, so the status code reveals which file IDs exist. The trace is accurate apart from a detail: line 16 belongs to delete_file and line 24 to rename_file, and the candidate's wording blurs them. Severity is low (existence oracle, not a bypass), and g.user comes from a client-settable header, so an unauthenticated caller can reach it.
